Anyone with access to your repository can read committed checkpoint data: the full prompt/response history and session metadata. Note that transcripts capture all tool interactions — including file contents, MCP server calls, and other data exchanged during the session. Per-checkpoint refs are less *visible* than a branch, but they are not less accessible: a `git fetch` of `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` reads them just as well.

If your repository is **public**, this data is visible to the entire internet.

### Keeping prompts out of checkpoints

Set `strategy_options.sync_prompts` to `false` to keep prompt content out of committed checkpoints, and therefore off the checkpoint remote:

```json
{ "strategy_options": { "sync_prompts": false } }
```

Put it in `.entire/settings.local.json` to opt out for yourself only, or in `.entire/settings.json` for everyone in the repository. The value must be a boolean; any other value fails settings load rather than being ignored.

With it disabled, each committed checkpoint omits `prompt.txt`, `full.jsonl`, `transcript.jsonl` and their image assets, subagent transcripts and task descriptions, AI summaries, review prompts, investigate topics, and skill-event native fields (which can record a slash command's arguments). Checkpoint metadata, attribution, files touched, token usage, and metrics are still recorded and synced. The consequences:

- `entire resume`, `entire checkpoint explain`, and search cannot show the conversation for those checkpoints.
- Local shadow branches still capture the session while it runs; they are never pushed and are cleaned up at condensation.
- Checkpoints written before the setting was disabled are not rewritten.
- `push_sessions: false` is the stronger switch: it stops checkpoint data from being pushed at all.

### What Entire redacts automatically

Entire automatically scans transcript and metadata content before writing it to a git object. Six always-on secret detection methods plus a configurable scanner layer (pattern matching, method 2 below) run during condensation, plus a conditional eighth pass for user-defined secret rules (see [Customizing redaction](#customizing-redaction) below), and an opt-in ninth pass for PII (see [Optional PII redaction](#optional-pii-redaction) below):

ets, tracking-ref readers, and blob hydration try candidates in order. Git-refs remote discovery ls-remotes every candidate **without** needing a dedicated `checkpoint_remote` and merges the listings. Local-ref writers stay **elected-remote-only**: `EnsurePrimaryRef`, the metadata-fetch advance, and `promoteRemoteTrackingPrimary` never act on the legacy tier (a stale origin feeding `SafelyAdvanceLocalRef` is the #1374-class hazard), keyed on the explicit election result, never on the chain's first entry. A remoteless repo keeps its "checkpoint absent" classification, which requires positive evidence (successful empty `git remote` listing, live ctx, readable settings without a `checkpoint_remote` key).
 - **Dedicated `checkpoint_remote` accepts `github` and `gitlab` providers**: `{"provider": "github"|"gitlab", "repo": "owner/repo"}` in `strategy_options.checkpoint_remote` (`entire configure --checkpoint-remote <provider>:<owner>/<repo>`). Nested GitLab groups (`group/subgroup/project`) pass validation; `CheckpointRemoteConfig.Owner()` takes the first path segment for the ownership vote, as the origin parser does. The checkpoint URL keeps the push remote's protocol and host (`checkpoint/remote/util.go:deriveCheckpointURLFromInfo`: SSH→SSH, HTTPS→HTTPS, `entire://`→same-cluster mirror when the origin's forge matches the provider); the provider's canonical host (`providerHost`) is used only when that derivation fails (`resolveProviderCheckpointURL`) or on the fetch side when `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` forces HTTPS. SSH/HTTPS derivation fails on purpose on a public forge of another provider (`checkPublicForgeMatchesProvider`: `github.com` for a gitlab store, `gitlab.com` for a github one), because that host names its provider and keeping it would send checkpoints — and a token — to the wrong forge; any other host (GitHub Enterprise, self-managed GitLab) is the user's own installation and is kept. That coercion is allow-listed by transport (`deriveTokenOriginURL` → `isTokenRewritableTransport`): only an origin whose host is the git host itself (`ssh`, `https`, `http`, `git`) is rewritten into a token-bearing HTTPS URL, because that URL becomes the fetch target and carries the credential. An `entire://` origin names an Entire cluster rather than a git endpoint, and `file://` names no host, so both are left as configured and no token is attached. The allow-list reads a transport, not a spelling: `gitremote.ParseURL` folds git's `git+ssh://` and `ssh+git://` aliases into `ssh` (`normalizeProtocol`), so one SSH remote cannot be admitted under one spelling and refused — silently, with no token and no SSH warning — under another; unrecognized `<x>+ssh` schemes are remote helpers to git and stay themselves so they still fail closed. The token is one Basic-auth header for both providers (`x-access-token:<token>`, `checkpoint/remote/git.go:appendCheckpointTokenEnv`); this relies on GitLab ignoring the Basic-auth username for Personal/Project Access Tokens — an external contract verified manually against gitlab.com, not enforced by CI. A gitlab `checkpoint_remote` is therefore direct transport only: `gitremote.hostToForge` maps only `github.com`, so the `entire://` mirror derivation never matches and falls back to `providerHost`. Everything else that is github-only has its own gate, not this one: trails (`trail_context_cache.go`, `info.Forge != ""` via `hostToForge`), `--issue-link` (`investigate/issuelink.go`, github.com hosts only), repo protection (control-plane repo `provider` enum, `github`/`entire`), and entire.io checkpoint discovery (server-side).
